1. Lines 172-191 use `while (redirects <= self.max_redirects)`, which permits one more redirect attempt than configured, so a client with `max_redirects = 5` can follow six redirect hops before returning `error.TooManyRedirects`. 

2. Lines 162-170 leak `current_host` if the second duplication for `current_path` fails, because the cleanup `defer` is installed only after both allocations succeed. 

3. Lines 176-186 leak the current `response` on the error path where `resolveUrl(...)` fails, because `response.deinit()` is called only after the new URL has already been allocated successfully. 

4. Lines 98-112 leak `path_copy` if `allocator.dupe(u8, base_host)` fails after the path allocation has already succeeded, because there is no `errdefer` protecting that earlier allocation. 

5. Lines 98-112 implement relative redirect resolution incorrectly, because path-relative, query-only, fragment-only, and empty `Location` values are not resolved against the current request URI and are instead forced into `"/{location}"` or treated as absolute-path replacements. 

6. Lines 98-105 also mishandle scheme-relative redirect targets like `//example.com/x`, because those are treated as ordinary local paths instead of network-path references with a new authority. 

7. Lines 40-80 misparse absolute URLs that omit `/` before a query or fragment, so inputs like `` or `` are treated as if the query or fragment were part of the authority. 

8. Lines 66-80 and 213 strip IPv6 brackets during parsing and then emit `Host: {s}` with the naked literal, which produces an invalid `Host` header for IPv6 authorities. 

9. Line 213 omits the port from the `Host` header even when the connection uses a non-default port, which breaks correct authority reporting for virtual hosts on alternate ports. 

10. Lines 194-232 never validate `req_path`, so the public API can emit malformed request targets such as empty paths, non-origin-form targets, or values containing illegal control bytes. 

11. Lines 26-31 reject only CR, LF, and NUL, so other ASCII control characters and DEL are still accepted in method, header, and path-adjacent fields even though they still make HTTP syntax invalid. 

12. Lines 214, 215, 223-231, and 307-333 hardcode request headers and always force `Connection: close`, which guarantees avoidable connection churn and extra handshakes instead of permitting reuse. 

13. Lines 223-229 allow `extra_headers` to duplicate headers that were already emitted earlier, so the client can generate conflicting `Host`, `Content-Length`, or `Connection` fields in the same request. 

14. Lines 249-280 do not apply `timeout_ms` to DNS resolution in `std.net.getAddressList`, so the advertised timeout does not actually bound the full request lifecycle. 

15. Lines 269-270 silently ignore `setsockopt` failures, so timeout configuration can fail without the caller knowing and socket behavior can diverge from the API contract. 

16. Lines 288-291 do not normalize send-side timeout behavior in plain transfers, because write errors propagate directly while only read-side `WouldBlock` is converted into `error.Timeout`. 

17. Lines 312-315 rescan the certificate bundle for every TLS request, which is a substantial repeated setup cost instead of reusable state. 

18. Lines 325-329 treat `error.TlsConnectionTruncated` and `error.ConnectionResetByPeer` as normal end-of-stream, so incomplete TLS responses can be accepted as if they were complete. 

19. Lines 296-300 do the same for plain HTTP by treating `ConnectionResetByPeer` as EOF, which can silently accept truncated responses. 

20. Lines 336-355 parse only the second token of the status line and never handle interim `1xx` responses, so a `100 Continue` or similar informational response can be returned instead of the final response. 

21. Lines 357-375 silently skip malformed header lines that lack a colon instead of rejecting the response, which makes invalid wire data look valid. 

22. Lines 371-375 collapse duplicate headers down to a single stored value, which loses legal repeated headers such as `Set-Cookie`. 

23. Lines 378-415 ignore `Content-Length`, so truncated non-chunked bodies are accepted whenever the peer closes early or the transport resets before the advertised body length is fully received. 

24. Lines 382-385 special-case only `chunked` and otherwise ignore other `Transfer-Encoding` values, so unsupported transfer codings are neither decoded correctly nor rejected explicitly. 

25. Lines 402-414 decode `Content-Encoding` only when the header is exactly `gzip`, `x-gzip`, or `deflate`, so valid multi-valued encodings such as `gzip, br` are handled incorrectly. 

26. Lines 417-423 return a decoded `body` while leaving headers like `transfer-encoding: chunked` or `content-encoding: gzip` unchanged, which makes the metadata inconsistent with the bytes exposed to callers. 

27. Lines 427-441 permit decompression up to 50 MiB even though raw transfer is capped at 20 MiB, so the memory limit policy is internally inconsistent and allows a much larger post-decode footprint than the transport limit implies. 

28. Lines 433-440 fall back from zlib decoding to raw deflate on any zlib error, which can mask genuine corruption and misclassify invalid compressed data as a different format. 

29. Lines 445-466 stop at the zero-length chunk without consuming and validating the trailer section and terminating CRLF, so malformed chunked bodies can be accepted as valid. 

30. Lines 154-191 resend the original method and body unchanged across 301, 302, and 303 redirects, so common redirect semantics such as converting a 303 follow-up into a GET are implemented incorrectly. 

that’s all.
